title: Why can squares, triangles and hexagons cover the whole plane?
description: Where tiles meet at a corner, their angles must fill three hundred and sixty degrees. Four square angles, six equilateral triangle angles or three regular hexagon angles fill a corner exactly, so each shape can cover the whole plane. Keeko's doubt, that circles tile the plane too, is struck.
teaching_notes: One idea: the angles at a meeting corner must add up to a full turn. Watch for students who think any neat shape, such as a circle, can tile the plane.

source: Explain why squares, equilateral triangles and regular hexag
video_script.why: The child sees that a shape covers the plane when its angle goes into a full turn exactly.
video_script.substitution: Four angles of 90 degrees, six of 60 degrees or three of 120 degrees each make a full turn of 360 degrees.
video_script.anchor: A flat surface covered with copies of one shape meeting at a corner, so that the angles at the corner fill a full turn.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks circles tile the plane too, because they are the neatest shape. But circles touch only at single points, and curved gaps are always left between them.
video_script.payoff_line: Each angle goes into three hundred and sixty degrees exactly.

final_answer.value: Each angle goes into 360° exactly: four 90°, six 60°, three 120°
final_answer.spoken: each angle goes into three hundred and sixty degrees exactly: four of ninety, six of sixty, three of one hundred and twenty

hold_back: Each angle goes into 360° exactly: four 90°, six 60°, three 120°
maths_rules: Where tiles meet at a corner, their angles must fill the full 360° with no gap and no overlap.
A square has angles of 90°, and 4 × 90 = 360, so four squares fill a corner.
An equilateral triangle has angles of 60°, and 6 × 60 = 360, so six triangles fill a corner.
A regular hexagon has angles of 120°, and 3 × 120 = 360, so three hexagons fill a corner.
Repeating these corners in every direction covers the whole plane.
Slip: circles touch only at single points, and curved gaps are left, so circles do not tile.
video_script.design: One meeting corner, shown three times: four squares, six triangles, three hexagons. Each angle is multiplied up to a full turn. The slip is the circle, which leaves curved gaps.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Covering a flat surface with shapes, with no gaps and no overlaps, is called tiling. The plane means the whole flat surface, going on in every direction.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>A triangle with three equal sides is called equilateral, and each of its angles is sixty degrees.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>A six sided shape with equal sides and equal angles is called a regular hexagon. Each of its angles is one hundred and twenty degrees.
